## What we covered

The model behind physician agency. Why we think financial incentives change
treatment, then a model where the physician sets both price and quantity, a
numerical example, and finally the case where the price is fixed
administratively.

## Key points

- Agency isn't special to medicine. It comes up whenever you hand a decision to
  someone who knows more than you do, which is why contracts and agency problems
  travel together in economics. The claim here is narrow. If you pay more for
  some things than others, then on average more of those things get done, and
  nothing about anyone behaving badly is required.
- We believe that because of a research design rather than a pattern in the
  data. Medicare redefined its geographic payment regions in the late 1990s, so
  a physician's payment formula changed while the physician changed nothing, not
  their location, not their practice, not their patients. Services shifted
  toward the ones that became better paid. The credibility comes from the change
  being in how the regions were drawn rather than in anything about the services
  themselves.
- The entire result comes from one gap. The physician decides based on their own
  marginal cost, while you decide based on the price you pay. Since price
  exceeds cost, the physician pushes care past where you would have stopped.
  Notice what isn't needed. Both sides know the same benefit function, so
  there's no information problem in this model at all.
- Past your own optimum, each additional unit has marginal benefit below price.
  Net benefit that would have been yours becomes profit instead, and the only
  thing that stops the process is your outside option, the point where you'd
  walk away.
- Fixed prices reverse the intuition, and this is the part worth being careful
  about. When the price is set administratively, cutting it increases the amount
  of care. It isn't that lower prices raise demand. It's that the constraint now
  has slack, so the physician can treat more before you'd walk away. Cutting
  fees to save money changes the quantity of care at the same time, and the
  savings are smaller than what you'd get by holding quantity fixed.
